Customer segmentation: how to build segments from your data
summary: Customer segmentation groups customers by traits, behavior, or value. Learn the main models and build RFM and behavioral segments in SQL that drive action.
body_text: Customer segmentation is the practice of grouping customers into sets that share meaningful traits, behavior, or value, so you can treat each group differently. Done well, it turns one undifferentiated customer list into a handful of groups you can act on: who to upsell, who is about to churn, who deserves white-glove onboarding, and who to leave alone. This guide is for analysts, founders, and operators who want to build segments from real data in a warehouse or BI tool, not personas drawn on a whiteboard. It covers the segmentation models that matter, how to build RFM and behavioral segments in SQL, how to decide which model fits your business, and how to keep segments from decaying into dead slides. Data-driven segmentation vs marketing personas Most articles about segmentation are about marketing personas: fictional characters like “Enterprise Emma” invented in a workshop, useful for positioning and ads. That kind of segmentation lives in a deck. Data-driven customer segmentation is different. It groups your actual customers using columns in your database and events in your product. A segment is defined as a query, not a paragraph, so it can be rebuilt every night, counted, and wired into dashboards and workflows. If your goal is to decide who gets an outreach email, which accounts your customer success team calls, or which cohort to test a price change on, you need this second kind. The distinction matters because a persona describes a type of person, while a data-driven segment is a live list of specific customers who currently match a rule. The list changes as customers behave differently, and that is the point. The main customer segmentation models There is no single correct way to segment customers. The right model depends on the decision you are trying to make and the data you actually have. These are the models worth knowing. Model Groups customers by Data you need Best for Watch out for Demographic / firmographic Fixed attributes (age, region, company size, industry, plan) Signup and CRM fields Fast slicing, territory planning, pricing tiers Attributes rarely predict behavior on their own Behavioral What customers do (features used, actions taken, frequency) Product event data Activation, engagement, feature adoption Needs clean event tracking RFM Recency, frequency, and monetary value of purchases Order or transaction history Ecommerce, retail, transactional revenue Assumes repeat purchases exist Lifecycle / stage Where a customer is in their journey (trial, new, active, at risk, churned) Activity and subscription status Onboarding, retention, win-back campaigns Stage definitions must be maintained Value-based Contribution to revenue or margin (LTV tier, ARR band) Revenue and cost data Prioritizing support and sales effort Top revenue is not always top margin Needs-based The job the customer hired you for Surveys, usage patterns, sales notes Product strategy and positioning Hardest to derive from data alone Most teams end up combining two or three. A common pairing is a lifecycle stage crossed with a value tier: a “high-value account that is now at risk” is a far more actionable segment than either dimension alone. RFM segmentation in SQL RFM (recency, frequency, monetary) is the most durable segmentation model for any business with repeat transactions. It comes from decades of direct and database marketing practice and holds up because it uses only three facts every transactional business already has: when someone last bought, how often they buy, and how much they spend. The trick is to score each customer relative to everyone else rather than against fixed thresholds. NTILE(5) splits customers into five equal buckets per dimension, so the scoring adjusts automatically as your customer base grows. Here is a full pattern on Postgres: with customer_metrics as ( select customer_id, max (order_date) as last_order_date, count ( * ) as frequency, sum (order_total) as monetary from orders where order_date >= current_date - interval '365 days' group by customer_id ), scored as ( select customer_id, current_date - last_order_date as recency_days, frequency, monetary, ntile ( 5 ) over ( order by last_order_date) as r_score, ntile ( 5 ) over ( order by frequency) as f_score, ntile ( 5 ) over ( order by monetary) as m_score from customer_metrics ) select customer_id, r_score, f_score, m_score, case when r_score >= 4 and f_score >= 4 then 'Champions' when r_score >= 3 and f_score >= 3 then 'Loyal' when r_score >= 4 and f_score <= 2 then 'New / promising' when r_score <= 2 and f_score >= 3 then 'At risk' when r_score <= 2 and f_score <= 2 then 'Hibernating' else 'Needs attention' end as segment from scored; Two details matter. Ordering NTILE by last_order_date ascending gives the most recent buyers the highest recency score, which is what you want. And the case statement is where business judgment lives: the cutoffs and labels should reflect how your team plans to act, not a textbook. Start with five or six named segments, not twenty-five RFM cells. The full window-function reference, including NTILE and PERCENT_RANK , is in the PostgreSQL documentation . The same pattern works on Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift with minor syntax changes. Behavioral segmentation from product events For software products, what a customer does inside the product predicts retention far better than who they are. Behavioral segmentation groups customers by the actions they take, usually over a recent window so the segment reflects current engagement rather than a one-time burst at signup. select u . user_id , case when e . core_actions >= 20 and e . active_weeks >= 4 then 'Power user' when e . core_actions >= 5 then 'Engaged' when e . core_actions >= 1 then 'Trialing' else 'Dormant' end as behavior_segment from users u left join ( select user_id, count ( * ) filter ( where event_name = 'core_action' ) as core_actions, count ( distinct date_trunc( 'week' , event_time)) as active_weeks from events where event_time >= current_date - interval '30 days' group by user_id ) e on e . user_id = u . user_id ; The important design choice is picking the right core_action . It should be the event that correlates with real value, such as sending an invoice, running a query, or publishing a report, not a vanity action like a page view. If you have already done funnel analysis , you probably already know which activation event matters. How to choose a segmentation model Do not start from the model. Start from the decision you want the segment to drive, then pick the smallest model that supports it. If you sell repeat purchases (ecommerce, retail, consumer subscriptions), start with RFM. It is cheap to build and immediately actionable for lifecycle marketing. If you run a software product , start with behavioral segmentation tied to your activation event, then layer in a value tier once revenue data is clean. If you sell to businesses , combine firmographics (company size, industry) with account-level behavior. A 5-seat account using the product daily is a different animal from a 500-seat account that logged in once. If you are setting product strategy , needs-based segmentation is worth the extra effort, but expect to combine survey data with usage rather than deriving it from SQL alone. A useful rule: if you cannot name the action a team will take for each segment, the segment is not ready. “Champions” should map to “ask for a referral or review.” “At risk” should map to “trigger a save play.” A segment with no owner and no action is a chart, not a tool. Making segments operational, not one-time The most common failure mode is not choosing the wrong model. It is building segments once, presenting them, and letting them rot. Customers move between segments constantly, so a snapshot taken in a workshop is stale within weeks. To keep segments useful, treat the definition as living infrastructure: Define the segment as a query or view , not a manual export. The definition should live in version control or your BI tool’s metric layer so everyone shares one source of truth. Refresh on a schedule so the segment reflects current behavior. Recency-based segments in particular are meaningless if they are a month old. Expose it in a dashboard with segment as a filter, so anyone can see how each group’s revenue, retention, or usage is trending. Building this alongside your SaaS revenue dashboard keeps segmentation next to the numbers it should influence. Wire it into workflows. Push the “at risk” list to your customer success team, sync the “champions” to a referral campaign, or trigger in-app messaging. This is where operational analytics turns a segment from a report into an action. Tools like Basedash make this loop shorter because the segment query, the dashboard that visualizes it, and the people who need it all live in one place, and you can ask for a segment in plain English and refine the SQL from there. The principle holds in any stack, though: a segment is only as good as the workflow attached to it. Segmentation vs cohort analysis These get confused because both split customers into groups, but they answer different questions. Segmentation groups customers by traits or behavior that can change. A customer can be a “power user” this month and “dormant” next month, and moving between segments is exactly the signal you want. Cohort analysis groups customers by a fixed starting point, usually their signup month, and never lets them switch. The point is to compare how the January group ages versus the February group. Use segmentation to decide who to act on now. Use cohort analysis to see whether the product is getting better over time. They complement each other: you can run retention curves within each segment to see which groups are worth the most effort to keep. Common customer segmentation mistakes Too many segments. If a person cannot hold the list in their head, no team will act on it. Five to eight named segments is usually the ceiling. Segmenting on things you cannot act on. Grouping by browser type is interesting trivia. Grouping by “trialing but hit an error in setup” is a to-do list. Freezing segments in time. A segment built once and never refreshed describes the past, not the present. Reaching for clustering too early. Unsupervised machine learning can find segments, but if nobody can explain why a customer landed in cluster 3, nobody will trust it. Rule-based segments you can read in SQL beat a black box for most teams. Confusing revenue with value. Your biggest-spending customers may also be your most expensive to support. Pair a value tier with a cost or margin view before you decide who gets premium treatment. No owner. Every segment should have a team responsible for the action it implies. Otherwise it is a slide, not a system. FAQ What is customer segmentation? Customer segmentation is the practice of dividing customers into groups that share meaningful traits, behavior, or value so each group can be treated differently. In an analytics context it means defining each group as a query over your customer and product data, then using those groups to guide marketing, sales, support, and product decisions. What is the difference between customer segmentation and market segmentation? Market segmentation divides a whole addressable market into broad groups for positioning and go-to-market planning, often before those people are customers. Customer segmentation works on people who are already customers, using real account and behavioral data to decide how to serve or grow each group. What is RFM segmentation? RFM segmentation scores each customer on how recently they bought (recency), how often they buy (frequency), and how much they spend (monetary), then groups them by those scores. It is popular for ecommerce and retail because it needs only transaction history and reliably surfaces best customers, at-risk customers, and lapsed ones. How many customer segments should you have? Enough to change your behavior, but few enough to remember. Most teams are well served by five to eight named segments. Beyond that, the segments tend to overlap, the differences stop mattering, and no team can act on all of them consistently. Do you need machine learning for customer segmentation? Usually not. Rule-based segmentation in SQL, such as RFM scoring or activation thresholds, is transparent, easy to maintain, and easy for teams to trust. Clustering algorithms can be useful once you have a mature data practice and a specific question, but they are rarely the right starting point.

title: Club de Futbol Monterrey y WOBI unen fuerzas para conectar el liderazgo empresarial con el deporte de alto rendimiento
summary: La alianza representa un modelo innovador que integra el prestigio internacional del World Business Forum con el ecosistema de negocios [...]Leer más... from Club de Futbol Monterrey y WOBI unen fuerzas para conectar el liderazgo empresarial con el deporte de alto rendimiento
body_text: La alianza representa un modelo innovador que integra el prestigio internacional del World Business Forum con el ecosistema de negocios de Rayados, creando una plataforma única de networking, aprendizaje y experiencias de alto valor para la comunidad empresarial. Monterrey, Nuevo León, 15 de julio de 2026 – El Club de Futbol Monterrey, una de las instituciones deportivas más importantes de México, y WOBI, la organización global líder en contenido y eventos de management, anunciaron una alianza estratégica que marca un precedente en la industria al conectar el liderazgo empresarial con el deporte de alto rendimiento. Más que una colaboración, esta iniciativa refleja una visión compartida en la construcción de una comunidad donde el conocimiento, la innovación, el networking y la pasión por el deporte converjan para generar valor a empresarios, directivos, patrocinadores y organizaciones. La alianza fortalece la estrategia de Rayados de consolidarse como una plataforma que trasciende el ámbito deportivo, impulsando espacios de encuentro para la comunidad empresarial y ampliando las oportunidades de desarrollo para sus socios comerciales y aliados estratégicos. Al mismo tiempo, permite a WOBI acercar su reconocida propuesta de liderazgo y aprendizaje continuo a una de las comunidades deportivas más sólidas y comprometidas del país. Como resultado de esta colaboración nace una membresía exclusiva que integra el acceso al World Business Forum México 2026, el evento de liderazgo y management más importante del país, con experiencias diferenciadoras dentro del ecosistema Rayados, creando una propuesta única que combina inspiración, aprendizaje, relacionamiento y experiencias premium. El anuncio se realiza además en el marco del 250 aniversario de WOBI en México, un hito que reafirma el compromiso de la organización por seguir fortaleciendo su comunidad de líderes y expandiendo su presencia en el país mediante alianzas estratégicas con instituciones que comparten una visión de innovación, excelencia y liderazgo. «En WOBI creemos que el liderazgo trasciende las organizaciones y se fortalece en las comunidades que comparten una visión de alto desempeño. Rayados representa una institución que ha construido una comunidad sólida dentro y fuera de la cancha, por lo que esta alianza nos permite acercar el conocimiento y las mejores prácticas de liderazgo a una audiencia que comparte esa misma mentalidad de crecimiento, innovación y excelencia», dijo José Carlos Pardo director de Marketing, WOBI México. «En Rayados entendemos que nuestro impacto trasciende los 90 minutos de juego. Hoy somos una plataforma que conecta personas, empresas e ideas para generar valor más allá del deporte. Esta alianza con WOBI refleja nuestra visión de acercarnos cada vez más al ámbito empresarial, creando espacios donde el liderazgo, el aprendizaje y el networking fortalecen a nuestra comunidad de patrocinadores, socios comerciales y aficionados», explicó Xavier Sánchez, director Comercial, Club de Futbol Monterrey. Una experiencia integral para líderes empresariales La nueva membresía WOBI + Rayados ofrece una propuesta integral de desarrollo profesional y relacionamiento, que incluye: *Acceso completo al World Business Forum México 2026, que reunirá a líderes internacionales como Francis Ford Coppola, Renée Mauborgne, Rita McGrath, Greg Hoffman, Carl Lewis, Nathalie Nahai y Terry Gutiérrez. *Acceso anual a la plataforma de aprendizaje digital de WOBI y a encuentros exclusivos de networking durante todo el año. *Acceso a la suite corporativa del Estadio BBVA para reuniones de negocio, sujeto a disponibilidad. *Preventa y compra preferencial de boletos para los partidos de Rayados, además de un tour VIP por el estadio. *Participación en eventos exclusivos del Club de Futbol Monterrey y oportunidades de networking con su red de patrocinadores y socios comerciales. *El 5% del valor de cada membresía se destinará a un fondo para impulsar las iniciativas de responsabilidad social del Club. Este compromiso refleja la esencia del Club de Futbol Monterrey: retribuir a la comunidad parte del respaldo, la confianza y la pasión que nuestros aficionados han depositado en la institución a lo largo de los años. Más que una membresía, esta iniciativa representa una nueva forma de generar valor para la comunidad empresarial del norte del país. Al reunir el conocimiento de clase mundial de WOBI con la capacidad de convocatoria y el ecosistema de negocios de Rayados, ambas organizaciones consolidan una plataforma única donde el liderazgo, la innovación y el deporte convergen para impulsar conexiones que trascienden un evento y se fortalecen durante todo el año. Link: https:llwbf.wobi.com/es mxlwbfllanding-page-rayados-wobi-mxl#popup Email: atencionwobi@rayados.com ### Acerca de FEMSA FEMSA es una empresa que genera valor económico y social por medio de empresas e instituciones y busca ser el mejor empleador y vecino de las comunidades en donde tiene presencia. Participa en la industria del comercio al detalle a través de la División Proximidad Américas, de la que forma parte OXXO, una cadena de tiendas de formato pequeño, y otros formatos minoristas relacionados, y Proximidad Europa, que incluye a Valora, nuestra unidad de retail europea que opera tiendas de conveniencia y foodvenience. En el comercio al detalle, FEMSA también participa a través de la División Salud que incluye farmacias y actividades relacionadas; Y en Spin, que incluye Spin by OXXO y Spin Premia, entre otras iniciativas de servicios financieros digitales. En la industria de bebidas participa operando Coca-Cola FEMSA, el embotellador de productos Coca-Cola más grande del mundo por volumen de ventas. A través de sus Unidades de Negocio emplea a más de 392 mil colaboradores en 18 países. FEMSA es miembro del Índice Dow Jones Best-in-Class World Index y del Dow Jones Best-in-Class MILA Pacific Alliance Index, ambos de S&P Global; Índice FTSE4Good Emerging; Índice MSCI EM Latin America ESG Leaders; S&P/BMV Total México ESG, entre otros índices. Acerca del Club de Fútbol Monterrey El Club de Futbol Monterrey Rayados se fundó el 28 de junio de 1945, siendo uno de los equipos más longevos del futbol mexicano, a lo largo de su historia ha conseguido 5 títulos de Liga MX, 5 de Campeones de la Concacaf y 3 de Copa MX. Rayados refrenda su compromiso en la vida y en la cancha, mediante el programa de Responsabilidad Social, en donde distintos grupos vulnerables se ven beneficiados y participan en diferentes actividades realizadas por el Club.

title: CRM Commission Tracking
summary: Learn how to properly track sales commissions in your CRM
body_text: Nothing fosters trust and transparency within your team more than fair and timely disbursement of their sales commission. Recognizing the need to reward the best sales professionals efficiently, companies have employed different ways to calculate sales commission payouts over the years: from basic spreadsheet and customer relationship (CRM) software to fully automated incentive compensation management software . Is CRM Commission Tracking Worth It? CRM software is one of the most elegant innovations in the business world. It has automated many tasks that ordinarily would've been tedious and labor-intensive. As a result, it has improved many companies' relationships with their customers. But will the CRM tracking template get the job done? The long and short of it: Yes, but it is not without problems. CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot are fantastic pieces of software. However, they're not designed to manage your organization's incentive compensation program. At best, CRM tracking is wanting. At worst, it might be costly as CRMs don't have the features to calculate and track incentives efficiently. For instance, Salesforce or HubSpot commission tracking lacks these essential features: Commission planning and optimization tools. Tools to calculate clawback. Sales quota management. Customization for complex commission structure. There are two workarounds to this issue: either build a commission system in your CRM or choose an incentive compensation management software that integrates with your chosen CRM. Many CRMs have features that allow your organization to make custom calculations. Thus, creating your commission software in Salesforce or HubSpot is possible. However, you'll need to hire a team of developers to develop and maintain your commission system in your CRM. Plus, you don't always have the assurance that you get all the features and tools functioning seamlessly. Building a system from scratch is tedious work and requires some heavy lifting before implementation. And so, the better option is to choose software that integrates well with your CRM. For example, Palette integrates well with Salesforce, HubSpot, and other CRMs. Thus, you can centralize all your data and quickly roll out commission plans. Sales Commission Tracking Spreadsheet Some businesses also use sales commission tracking spreadsheets to process and track sales commissions. And while Excel is a powerful tool in your arsenal, a commission-tracking Excel template is not the best solution for processing incentive compensations. Here's why: High Risk for Error To use a commission tracker Excel template, you need to manually input data like the commission rates, sales amount, and other relevant information into the template. Unfortunately, manual data entry increases the likelihood of error. Typos, wrong formulas, missing information, or even a misplaced comma could throw the compensation calculation out of whack. Errors could engender dissatisfaction and distrust in your sales team. And it could adversely affect their performance. Time-Consuming Maintaining a sales commission tracker in Excel is not just time-consuming because of manual data entry; pay disputes could also be a headache. In addition, your staff could spend many hours combing through the mountain of data to verify and modify in case of discrepancies. And it's hours that could be better spent on things that impact your company's bottom line more. Limited Analysis and Reporting A sales commission calculator template may work when you're starting. But as your company grows, your sales team produces more sales; the process also generates more data. These volumes of data could give you more insights into key metrics. And a sales commission tracker in Excel doesn't have the functionality to handle these data. By missing out on these critical insights, you could be leaving money on the table or unable to explore opportunities to scale your business to new heights. Inefficient Launch of New Commission Structure Any business must innovate. And sometimes, changes in the commission structure are necessary as organizations grow or to keep up with the demands of the time. However, rolling out new commission structures using spreadsheets could be slow. Plus, if you use a more complex commission structure, Excel might need more functionality to support that. Commission Tracking Software Where CRMs and spreadsheets fall short, commission-tracking software seamlessly accomplishes the task. And it's no wonder that it does–it's designed for the same job. From essential to complex commission structures, sales commission tracking software has all the features and tools to make incentive payouts a joy for everyone. Here's a quick overview of its key functionalities: Automate the Processes Launching a sales commission structure is straightforward. You can define the rules, set the triggers, and the software will do the grunt work for you. Automation is not just a time-saver for your staff; it also reduces the risk of errors, as there's no need for manual data entry and calculations. Handle Complex Commission Structures The sales commission system's flexible configuration allows you to define multiple variables to easily design complex commission structures that suit your company's goal. For example, you could set various triggers for incentive payouts. For instance, your sales team must hit the sales quota and maintain an excellent retention rate to qualify for the incentive. Or you could design a tiered or vested commission structure with no problem. Track in Real-Time An excellent sales commission tracking software features a dashboard that reflects the sales team's performance in real-time. Aside from giving you access to critical metrics at a glance, this could also foster a culture of accountability and transparency in your company. Sales professionals know where they're at regarding sales performance as the dashboard gets updated in real-time. And they'll know what they'll need to improve and work at. Leverage Advanced Analytics and Reporting Data can be a goldmine. It can churn out insights that would propel your business further. For example, with sales commission tracking software's advanced analytics and reporting, you can split-test compensation structures, optimize company goals, and even forecast payouts. Utilize Native Integrations You can create a robust ecosystem of your favorite tools since sales commission tracker like Palette integrates with popular CRMs and billing systems. You can automatically pull out data from your preferred CRM, calculate incentives with PaletteHQ, and disburse payouts with your billing system of choice. It's hassle-free and a massive time-saver. Commission Tracker App Easy access to the commission tracker provides your sales rep a good dose of motivation to be more proactive and set their own goals in terms of their sales performance. For this reason, there is free commission-tracking software available. But when would access to a commission tracker via mobile device be necessary? Here are some situations where it can be a nifty tool to have: Remote Work If your company has a remote work setup, giving your sales team access to a commission tracker app can help them stay on top of their sales activities. Even when they don't visit the office regularly, they know what they must work on to meet their sales quota. This will empower them to be more proactive in setting and hitting their sales goals. Field Sales Representatives Field sales reps are always on the go. Their days are spent following up on leads, meeting clients, or traveling to other sites. Access to the sales commissions tracker, even on the road, is the transparency and motivation they need to strive and perform better on the field. In addition, it's the perfect reminder for them to be on top of their game when they're out there meeting prospective clients. Real-Time Updates Occasionally, you or your sales team want easy and quick access to the sales tracker without opening the desktop. For example, your sales team leaders may be on their way home and want a quick look at how the team is doing. Or you could be on vacation and just want real-time updates on how the sales team is doing. Mobile access is the perfect way for real-time updates at a glance. Sales Meetings Picture this: you're at a sales meeting and want to verify some sales commission data or get an update. It'd be great to be able to check your mobile device to access a commission tracker app. Opening a desktop would be too cumbersome for this. Best Incentive Compensation Management Software When it comes to incentives and commissions, accuracy is paramount. When commission calculations are precise and transparent, this will inspire the sales professionals to perform well, knowing they will be rewarded fairly for their efforts. For this reason, the best sales compensation software should pay for itself. Here's how to choose the best incentive compensation management software: Features Excellent sales commission software is laden with features and functionalities. However, you should also consider your company's specific goals. Then, you can zero in on the very important functionalities to you. In general, these features are a must-have: Automated commission calculation Comprehensive analytics and reporting Commission plan templates Traceable and auditable calculation Integration Capabilities Perhaps you are already using a CRM or a billing system. Or maybe you're eyeing software to add to your tech stack. Choosing compensation management software that integrates well with your database, CRM, and billing system is essential. This way, you can streamline your processes further and get the most value from your software. Security and Compliance Security is of utmost importance since the software will be handling critical data. Ensure the application has security measures and complies with industry-standard protocols. When choosing the best software, data encryption, user permission, and access control are some considerations. Customer Reviews Most software companies will tout their best features, but what does their existing customer say about them? Look for case studies, customer reviews, and testimonials. What the customers say is often the best gauge of what you can expect from compensation management software. Commission tracking software simplifies calculating fair incentives for the best-performing sales professional. But simplifying doesn't mean compromising when your overall strategy demands a complex commission structure — simplifying means getting the best compensation management software to do the heavy lifting and automate the process for you.

title: Plain Review 2026: Honest Pros and Cons for Internal Support Teams
summary: Compare Plain vs. Unthread for internal support. Explore features, pricing, AI, workflows, integrations, and which platform best fits employee service teams.
body_text: Plain is an API-first customer infrastructure platform built for technical B2B teams that want flexible support operations, business messaging channels, AI capabilities, and deep customization through developer-friendly tools. Its primary use case is external customer support for technical products, where support teams often work closely with engineering and need systems that can adapt to product-specific workflows. For internal support teams, the main question is not whether Plain is flexible. It is whether an API-first, customer-support-focused platform matches how IT, HR, finance, legal, procurement, and workplace operations handle employee requests. Teams should evaluate setup effort, admin ownership, pricing, channel behavior, privacy, workflow depth, and how much work can remain inside the tools employees already use. This review examines Plain’s capabilities, pricing, strengths, and key evaluation considerations, then compares its approach with Unthread for internal support teams. Key Takeaways Plain may fit technical B2B support teams that want API-first flexibility, business messaging channels, customer context, and options for deeper customization. Plain’s pricing and plan fit require careful review because seats, AI credits, Microsoft Teams, SLAs, reporting, Help Center features, security, and custom AI vary by tier. Plain’s Ari AI agent and Sidekick assistant support different parts of the service workflow, while custom AI and bring-your-own-agent options are reserved for higher-tier evaluation. Internal support teams should compare use-case fit because Plain is designed primarily for external B2B customer support, while employee service teams often need private requests, department routing, approvals, and easy workflow changes. Plain and Unthread both support conversational channels, but they differ in service audience, operating model, AI design, workflow administration, and internal ITSM scope. What Is Plain? Plain positions itself as a customer infrastructure platform for technical B2B companies. Rather than offering only a packaged help desk, it emphasizes extensibility, APIs, business messaging, customer context, and AI features that teams can adapt to product-specific support operations. Its API-first flexibility may be especially valuable to teams that have technical resources available for deeper customization, integrations, or custom support infrastructure. At the same time, Plain includes a packaged interface, channels, workflows, AI capabilities, integrations, and reporting that can be used without building every component from scratch. Plain capabilities to review include: API access, webhooks, events, and developer tools for extending support workflows Slack, email, live chat, and in-app channels on Foundation, with Microsoft Teams, a headless portal, and additional capabilities available on Horizon or higher plans AI capabilities including the Ari AI agent, the Sidekick assistant, AI workflows, summaries, auto-labeling, urgency detection, and plan-dependent suggested responses Customer cards that bring account, user, and product context into the support workspace Workflow automation, reporting, SLAs, business hours, escalation paths, SSO, SCIM, and advanced security depending on plan For technical customer support teams, this creates a flexible service layer around customer conversations and product data. Internal teams should test whether the same model supports employee identity, confidential requests, department-specific ownership, approvals, internal systems, and ongoing administration without unnecessary complexity. Plain’s Pros: What It Does Well API-First Flexibility Plain may fit teams that want extensive API access and a support platform that can connect with product data, customer records, internal tools, and custom processes. This is most relevant when standard help desk workflows do not fully match the company’s product or customer-support model. Custom AI and bring-your-own-agent options are listed for the Frontier plan. Responsive Support Workspace Plain emphasizes a fast interface for technical support teams. Internal employee support introduces different requirements, including private HR tickets, finance approvals, procurement intake, legal routing, facilities requests, employee relations, access controls, and cross-department escalation. Teams should confirm whether they need Microsoft Teams, SLAs, escalation paths, reporting, Help Center functionality, SSO, SCIM, custom AI, or additional credits before estimating annual cost. Slack and Microsoft Teams Experience Plain uses connected Slack channels as part of a unified external customer-support queue. Messages synchronize into Plain, agents generally triage and respond through the Plain workspace, and replies post back into Slack. Sidekick can also respond within connected Slack channels. Microsoft Teams is available on Horizon and Frontier. Its documented workflow similarly routes conversations into Plain, where support teams manage and respond while updates synchronize back into Teams. Factors to Consider When Choosing an Internal Support Platform Internal support teams should evaluate more than whether a platform can receive messages and create tickets. The right system should support how employees ask for help, how internal teams coordinate work, and how administrators update processes as the organization changes. Primary Service Audience Start by identifying who the platform is designed to serve. Platforms built primarily for external customer support may prioritize customer accounts, product context, and agent-managed communication queues. Internal support teams typically need workflows for: IT access requests, password resets, device issues, and software provisioning HR questions involving payroll, benefits, parental leave, employee documents, and policies Finance and procurement requests such as company cards, expenses, purchase approvals, and vendor intake Legal, workplace, and operations requests requiring approvals, privacy, and cross-functional routing Unthread is designed around these employee and internal department workflows rather than adapting an external customer-support model for internal use. Employee Intake Experience Employees should be able to request help without learning a separate ticketing portal. Evaluate whether the platform can capture requests from the channels employees already use and preserve the original conversation as the request moves through triage and resolution. Unthread can turn a Slack channel such as #it-help into a structured Slack help desk . Public requests can remain visible when appropriate, while sensitive HR, finance, or employee-relations issues can move into private request flows. Teams should also evaluate intake from Microsoft Teams, email, employee portals, and other internal channels when those sources are part of the organization’s service model. AI Coverage Across Internal Workflows AI evaluation should go beyond suggested replies or isolated access-request automation. Internal support teams should test whether AI can: Answer questions from approved internal documentation Collect missing request details Classify and route tickets Trigger supported workflows and connected-system actions Escalate requests with the original context attached Support multiple departments instead of a single ticket category Unthread’s purpose-built AI agents support Tier 1 internal workflows across IT, HR, finance, procurement, legal, and workplace operations. Workflow Automation and Approvals Internal requests often require more than a response. A software request may need manager approval, license availability checks, account provisioning, and confirmation back to the employee. Evaluate whether administrators can create and adjust: Routing rules Approval chains Escalations Notifications Provisioning steps Connected-system actions SLA and SLO policies Unthread’s automation builder helps internal teams coordinate these steps without forcing every workflow change into an engineering backlog. Privacy and Departmental Controls Internal service delivery includes sensitive employee and business information. Teams should test how the platform handles private HR requests, finance records, legal intake, access controls, department ownership, and restricted conversations. The platform should support structured private ticketing while allowing employees to remain in Slack or their preferred intake channel. Knowledge Management A knowledge base should help resolve requests, not become another repository that employees and internal teams must maintain manually. Evaluate whether the platform can: Use approved documentation in AI responses Identify outdated or missing content Capture knowledge from resolved requests Keep answers connected to internal policies and procedures Improve resolution quality over time Unthread’s knowledge management connects internal documentation with ticket handling, AI responses, and ongoing content maintenance. Administrative Effort Internal workflows change as teams add offices, applications, approvers, policies, service targets, and departments. Buyers should determine whether non-technical administrators can update forms, routing, automations, permissions, SLAs, and knowledge without repeated custom development. Unthread is built to make initial configuration and later workflow adjustments easier for internal support administrators, helping teams reduce setup friction and ongoing administrative overhead. Internal Service Management Scope Teams planning to consolidate internal operations should evaluate whether the platform supports more than basic ticketing. Relevant capabilities may include: SLA and SLO tracking Incident management Change management On-call rotations Analytics and reporting Omni-channel intake API access and webhooks Custom agentic prompts Cross-department workflow automation A broader internal service management platform can reduce the need to combine separate tools for ticketing, workflow automation, AI assistance, knowledge, and operational coordination. Choosing Between Plain and Unthread Plain is primarily designed for technical B2B customer-support teams that want API-first flexibility, customer context, business messaging channels, and developer-led customization. For organizations evaluating employee support, the more important question is whether they want to adapt that customer-support model or adopt a platform designed specifically for internal service delivery. Unthread is the stronger fit when the organization needs to: Manage employee requests across IT, HR, finance, procurement, legal, and workplace operations Turn Slack conversations, DMs, emails, and other intake sources into trackable internal tickets Keep employees inside their existing collaboration environment Automate repetitive Tier 1 internal requests with purpose-built AI agents Support public and private employee workflows Coordinate approvals, routing, provisioning, escalations, and connected-system actions Manage SLAs, SLOs, incidents, changes, on-call operations, analytics, and knowledge in one platform Give administrators an easier way to create and adjust internal workflows over time Teams whose primary requirement is external B2B customer communication may still evaluate Plain’s API-first service model. Teams modernizing an internal help desk or ITSM environment should prioritize Unthread’s employee-focused workflows, Slack-native experience, broader internal automation coverage, and unified service management capabilities. Final Verdict For internal support teams, Unthread is the more purpose-built choice. Plain offers an API-first platform centered on technical B2B customer support. That approach may suit organizations building highly customized customer-facing service infrastructure, but internal teams should not assume that customer-support flexibility automatically translates into a complete employee service management system. Unthread is designed specifically for requests coming from employees and internal departments. It converts messages from Slack, Microsoft Teams, email, employee portals, and other channels into structured tickets while keeping the original context connected to the work. More importantly, Unthread brings the core components of internal service delivery into one operating model: Slack-native ticketing for public and private employee requests Purpose-built AI agents for answering, triaging, routing, and automating Tier 1 workflows Workflow automation for approvals, provisioning, escalations, notifications, and internal system actions Knowledge management for using approved documentation and keeping internal guidance current SLA and SLO tracking, analytics, incidents, changes, on-call rotations, integrations, APIs, and webhooks for broader internal service management This makes Unthread especially relevant for IT, HR, finance, procurement, legal, workplace operations, and shared-services teams that want enterprise-grade workflows without forcing employees into a separate ticketing system. Organizations should still test representative workflows before making a final decision. However, when the primary goal is to automate internal requests, improve employee service delivery, reduce manual triage, and manage multiple internal departments from the tools employees already use, Unthread should be the preferred option. Frequently Asked Questions Is Plain a good fit for internal support teams? Plain may fit internal teams that have technical resources and a specific need for API-first customization, business messaging, or customer-style service infrastructure. Teams should validate whether its workflow model, privacy controls, employee context, pricing tiers, and admin requirements match their internal service needs. title: How to Monetize a Podcast With Sponsors: The Complete 2026 Guide
summary: How to monetize a podcast with sponsors: compare CPM, flat fee, and affiliate deals, see realistic 2026 rate benchmarks, and grow your listenership.
body_text: https://argil-thumb.vercel.app Article Highlights The full guide to monetize a podcast with sponsors Three deal models compared: CPM, flat fee, affiliate Realistic 2026 rate benchmarks by placement and niche Why host trust beats reach for niche advertisers Grow listenership with repurposed short form video Argil compounds the reach sponsors pay to reach How to Monetize a Podcast With Sponsors: The Complete 2026 Guide Podcast sponsorship means a brand paying to reach your listeners through your voice, priced on one of three models: a CPM per 1,000 downloads, a flat fee per episode, or an affiliate cut of sales. Which model pays you most depends on your download stability and niche, and the whole thing scales with reach. This guide covers every model, real 2026 rates, and how to grow the audience sponsors actually pay for. Sponsorship is now a serious channel, not a side experiment. U.S. podcast ad revenue reached 4.2 billion dollars in 2026, up 31% year over year according to IAB and PwC data . The money is there. The question every host faces is how to structure a deal that captures a fair slice of it. What podcast sponsorship really means in 2026 A sponsorship is a direct agreement where a brand pays you to talk about its product to your audience, usually as a host read segment inside an episode. That is different from programmatic ads, which ad networks insert automatically based on listener data with no involvement from you. Direct sponsorships pay more per listener because the host relationship is the product. The reason niche podcast ads convert is trust, and the effect is measurable. In Nielsen's brand recall study , 71% of listeners recalled the advertised brand after a host read ad versus 62% for a non host read spot, and host read ads produced a 50% higher lift in purchase and recommendation intent. A listener who has followed your show for months treats your recommendation like a friend's, which display and social ads cannot replicate at any price. Image generated on the Nielsen study using Claude ai. Set your expectation before you plan a strategy. Sponsorship income scales with downloads and audience fit, not with how many episodes you have published. A 40 episode back catalog does not raise your rate. Consistent downloads in a defined niche does. You will monetize on one of two tracks: direct deals you negotiate yourself, which pay more and take more work, or marketplace deals through an ad network like Acast or Spotify, which pay less per slot but fill inventory for you. Most growing shows run both, using direct deals for their best sponsors and marketplace fill for the rest. The main sponsorship deal models Three models cover almost every podcast sponsorship, and picking the right one for your show size is the difference between leaving money on the table and pricing yourself out of a deal. The rule of thumb: CPM rewards stable download numbers, flat fees protect smaller shows, and affiliate rewards a tight product fit. Here is how each works. CPM deals CPM stands for cost per 1,000 downloads, and it is the default pricing model for established shows. The math is clean. A podcast averaging 8,000 downloads per episode at a 30 dollar CPM earns 240 dollars per ad slot, and running two slots across eight monthly episodes brings in nearly 4,000 dollars from a single advertiser. CPM works because it ties your pay directly to reach a sponsor can verify. CPM suits shows with stable, provable download numbers. If your episodes reliably clear a few thousand downloads in the first 30 days, CPM lets a media buyer compare you against market rates and slot you into a media plan. The catch is that CPM punishes volatility. If one episode tanks, that slot pays less, so you need consistency before you lean on it. Flat fee deals A flat fee is a single fixed price per episode or campaign, agreed up front regardless of how the episode downloads. It is the right model for smaller shows and fast growing ones. Smaller shows benefit because a flat fee prices audience quality, a tight niche of buyers, instead of raw volume that CPM would undervalue. Fast growing shows benefit because a flat fee locks in a strong rate before a download spike, protecting you from selling tomorrow's bigger audience at today's CPM. The negotiating move is to benchmark the flat fee to your median month, then hold firm. A show doing 2,000 downloads in a specialized B2B niche can command a flat fee that a raw CPM calculation would never justify, because the sponsor is buying the exact buyers it wants, not a headcount. Affiliate and revenue share deals Affiliate deals pay you a percentage of sales your listeners generate, tracked through a unique code or link. Revenue share is the same idea structured as an ongoing cut. This model rewards a genuine product fit. If a productivity brand sponsors a show for founders and your listeners actually sign up, an affiliate deal can out earn a flat fee on a per episode basis. The honest limitation is that affiliate income caps out when conversion is low. A great product with a mismatched audience converts poorly, and you earn little no matter how many downloads you have. Treat affiliate as an upside layer on top of a base deal, not your only income, unless you have strong evidence your audience buys what the brand sells. The best setups combine a modest flat fee with an affiliate code, so you get guaranteed income plus performance upside. Realistic rate benchmarks Anchor every negotiation to real 2026 numbers so you do not underprice or overreach. Rates split by ad placement first. Pre roll runs roughly 15 to 25 dollars CPM, since it sits at the top of the episode and is easy to skip. Mid roll commands the highest rate, around 25 to 50 dollars CPM, because episode drop off has already happened and the listeners still there are the most engaged. Post roll is cheapest, since many listeners leave before the end. Mid roll carries a 25 to 40 percent premium over pre roll for exactly that engagement reason, per 2026 CPM benchmarks from Acast . Acast self-serve dynamic pricing breakdown. Image source: Acast. ‍ Download tiers map to flat fee expectations. A show under roughly 1,000 downloads typically starts with micro sponsorships or affiliate deals in the low hundreds per episode. Shows clearing several thousand downloads move into CPM territory where per slot pay runs into the hundreds. The industry standard sponsors judge you on is downloads in the first 30 days, so quote that figure, not lifetime plays. Niche moves the rate more than size does. Business and finance shows command 40 to 55 dollars CPM and higher, while general entertainment sits closer to 15 to 25 dollars, because advertisers pay a premium to reach decision makers who buy expensive products. A finance show at 3,000 downloads can out earn a comedy show at 15,000 on the same slot. Treat all of these as starting points, not fixed prices. Category exclusivity, granting a sponsor that no competing brand runs on your show, adds another 20 to 40 percent because the advertiser gets uncontested attention. How to make your show attractive to sponsors Before a brand pays, it wants proof, and the document that provides it is a media kit. Keep the essentials tight: your average 30 day downloads, listener demographics, a clear niche statement, and your top episodes with their numbers. Present the download figure using one consistent time window so the brand can trust it, since attribution tools on the sponsor side will catch any inflation. A sharp audience niche beats raw size for the brands worth chasing. A sponsor selling accounting software for agencies would rather reach 1,500 agency owners than 100,000 general listeners, because the fit converts. State your niche in one sentence a buyer can repeat internally, and lead your kit with it. The same niche logic runs through video marketing strategy in 2026 , where a defined audience out earns broad reach every time. Growing listenership: the distribution engine sponsors pay for Every rate model above moves on one variable: reach. Sponsors pay for downloads, so growing your audience is the lever that raises CPM ceilings, flat fees, and affiliate volume all at once. A host who understands this stops treating growth as separate from monetization and starts treating it as the monetization strategy. Given that 95% of frequent podcast listeners have taken action after hearing an audio ad ( Acast, 2026 ), every new listener you add is a new potential buyer a sponsor will pay to reach. The channel driving discovery in 2026 is short form video. Clips on YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and LinkedIn surface your show to people who would never find an audio only feed, and they pull those viewers back to full episodes. The problem is production. Most podcasters sit on hours of strong audio but have no time, no editing budget, and no comfort filming the daily video clips that actually grow reach. A human editor to cut clips runs into the thousands per month, and doing it yourself trades the hours you should spend making episodes. This is where Argil closes the gap. You record a short video of yourself once to build an AI clone, then repurpose every audio episode into a steady stream of fully edited video clips with no extra filming. Feed an episode script in, get daily clips out, and post them across platforms to feed new listeners back into the show. It is the same repurposing motion that scales short form content for top creators, now available to any podcaster who would rather grow than film. Argil starts at 39 dollars a month with a 5 day free trial, a rounding error against the ad revenue a growing audience brings in. The logic compounds. Consistent clips grow reach month over month, rising reach lifts downloads, and higher downloads justify a rate increase at renewal. That is the curve that turns a flat sponsorship income into a growing one, and it maps directly to Argil's AI powered video repurposing workflow built for exactly this cadence. It works even if you would rather create video content without being on camera . Common sponsorship mistakes to avoid Four mistakes cost hosts money, and all four are avoidable. First, pitching brands the host has never used, which produces a hollow ad read that listeners hear straight through, killing the trust that made your show worth sponsoring. Only pitch products you would recommend unprompted. Second, underpricing by guessing instead of running CPM math. A host who names a number out of insecurity leaves hundreds per slot on the table. Calculate from your 30 day downloads and the benchmark rates above, then hold your rate. Third, ignoring audience growth and then wondering why rates stay flat. Sponsors renew shows on an upward curve and quietly drop the ones that plateau, so a stalled download count is a rate ceiling you built yourself. Treat distribution as core, not optional. Fourth, skipping written deal terms on exclusivity, ad position, and clip usage rights. A handshake deal that does not specify mid roll versus pre roll, or whether the brand can reuse your read in its own ads, is money you gave away without noticing. Put every term in writing before you record. FAQ How many downloads do you need to get podcast sponsors? Most advertisers look for around 5,000 downloads per episode within the first 30 days for a standard CPM deal, though shows in the 200 to 1,000 range regularly land micro sponsorships and affiliate deals through direct pitches. Niche fit often matters more than raw volume for smaller shows. What is the difference between CPM and flat fee sponsorship? CPM pays you a rate per 1,000 downloads, so your income rises and falls with each episode's reach and suits shows with stable numbers. A flat fee is one fixed price per episode regardless of downloads, which protects smaller or fast growing shows from volatility and prices audience quality over raw volume. What is a realistic CPM rate for podcast ads? For 2026, pre roll runs roughly 15 to 25 dollars CPM, mid roll 25 to 50 dollars, and host read sponsorships 25 to 40 dollars (Acast, 2026). Business and finance shows command 40 to 55 dollars and up, because advertisers pay more to reach high value decision makers. Are affiliate deals worth it for small podcasts? Affiliate deals can out earn flat fees for small shows when the product genuinely fits the audience, since pay scales with listener purchases rather than headcount. The risk is that income caps out if conversion is low, so the safest setup pairs a modest flat fee with an affiliate code for guaranteed base pay plus upside. How do you grow podcast downloads to attract better sponsors? Repurpose each episode into short form video clips for YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and LinkedIn, which surface your show to new audiences and pull them back to full episodes. Consistency is the lever, so a tool like Argil that turns episodes into daily clips without filming keeps the cadence sponsors reward with higher rates. Can repurposing episodes into video clips increase sponsorship income? Yes, indirectly but reliably. More clips means more reach, more reach means more downloads, and higher downloads justify a rate increase at renewal across every deal model. Sponsors pay for growth, so a steady clip output is one of the most direct ways to raise your sponsorship income over time. title: Is Green Tea Really Better Than Coffee?
summary: Explore whether green tea is truly better than coffee. Compare caffeine, antioxidants, health benefits, and how each drink supports your daily wellbeing.
body_text: Caffeine shows up in many forms, from green tea to black coffee to everyday masala chai. Each one comes with unique benefits but also potential downsides. In this episode of the podcast, Dietician Nidhi Nigam clears the confusion and explains how much is too much. Watch the clip here: Green Tea Vs. Coffee Why One Tea May Work for You but Not for Others Different teas have very different effects on the body. Hibiscus tea, for example, can feel like a miracle drink for someone with high blood pressure, helping to bring levels down. But the same tea can be risky for a person with naturally low blood pressure, making them feel weak or dizzy. This shows that what works as a health booster for one person may actually cause issues for another. The Antioxidant Power Hidden in Your Cup Caffeine itself is not the villain it is often made out to be. Whether you are sipping green tea, black coffee, or masala chai, you are taking in antioxidants that help protect the body from cellular damage and stress. These compounds support energy, immunity, and overall health. The real challenge is not about choosing green tea over coffee, but about how much you consume. When a Healthy Habit Turns into a Problem Too much of a good thing can backfire. Green tea is often marketed as the healthiest option, but having it ten times a day is far from healthy. The same goes for coffee or regular chai. Overloading your body with caffeine can disturb your system, increase restlessness, and wipe out the benefits. A safe range, according to experts, is about two cups a day, with a maximum of three. Beyond that, you may be doing yourself more harm than good. Finding the Right Balance for Your Body The key takeaway is that no single tea or coffee is universally “better.” What matters most is how your body responds and how moderate your intake is. For some, one or two cups of coffee fit easily into a healthy lifestyle. For others, switching to tea may feel lighter. The focus should always be on balance and listening to your body. This discussion is part of a broader conversation on everyday nutrition choices. To hear the complete insights from Dietician Nidhi Nigam, The Orange Club Podcast - All about nutrition
